display.title: Chitas: The Best Cure
display.summary_short: Before Yud-Aleph Nissan, why the Rebbe urges daily Chitas and Rambam, and how a rosh yeshiva who could no longer walk was healed after taking on Chitas at the Rebbe's word.
display.summary_long: After the song 'I Believe in Hashem', the storyteller prepares for Yud-Aleph Nissan with the Rebbe's daily study campaigns: Chitas (Chumash, Tehillim and Tanya) and the daily Rambam in its three tracks. The Rambam's 83 sections of halachah match the numerical value of machlah, sickness, so learning them protects us, and the Rambam unites all Jews in studying the whole Torah. Then comes a story from 1954. A rosh yeshiva in Yerushalayim, too ill in his legs to stand, is carried to his son's wedding in his bed and tells the guests why. As a yeshiva student in Poland, he and his friends debated too long before helping a wagon driver whose horse was choking, and the horse died. A town drunkard sleeping in the shul warned them that if they would not go, they would not be able to stand on their feet. That man turned out to be a hidden tzaddik, with beautiful tefillin and deep writings, and a miraculous space opened beside a great tzaddik's grave for his burial. A wedding guest wrote to the Rebbe, who answered that the rosh yeshiva should take on the Frierdiker Rebbe's Chitas and spread it to his students. Half a year later he was sitting at his table and getting better every day.
display.lesson: Learn Chitas and Rambam every day, as the Rebbe asks; it brings blessing and healing. Never put off helping someone in need, even a person or animal in trouble.

advisories.note: A rosh yeshiva cannot walk and doctors consider amputating his legs; he recovers.
A horse dies when help comes too late; a hidden tzaddik foretells his own passing and is buried.
The hidden tzaddik is known in town as a drunkard.
